Against a quick proof by exhaustion

evidence.excerpt: A foundationally justified belief (henceforth simply: ‘foundational belief’) is one that does not depend on any other beliefs for its justification.
Rightly skeptical, you wonder this time what reason I have for believing that palm lines have anything whatsoever to do with length of life.
Against this, the proponent of PIJ might ask us to consider an amendment to the case.
If all justification is inferential, then for someone S to be justified in believing some proposition P, S must be in a position to legitimately infer it from some other proposition E1.
And so, if all justification were inferential, no one could be justified in believing anything at all to any extent whatsoever.

The epistemic regress argument for foundationalism thus needs an additional premise, though one that all but the most radical skeptics would accept: that epistemic justification is in principle possible for beings like us.
A number of philosophers (among them foundationalists) would argue that the second clause of PIJ confuses levels of epistemic questions.

Similarly, even though there is in fact a connection between ingesting hemlock and dying, a person who had no reason to believe that ingesting hemlock would bring about death has no justification for believing that someone (who has just ingested hemlock) is about to die.
There are responses to the charge of vicious regress facing anti-foundationalists.
According to coherentism about epistemic justification, beliefs are justified “holistically” rather than in a linear, piecemeal way.
Some forms of coherentism might complicate our taxonomy.
For some further discussion of infinitism and challenges to it, see Klein and Turri (2014).

sources.annotation: Separates the regress arguments, classical and modest foundations, and objections to non-inferential support.

evidence.excerpt: The coherentist might be thought to propose that nothing prevents the regress from proceeding in a circle.
If she did justify \(A\) in terms of \(C\) nonetheless, her move would lack any justificatory force whatsoever.
This is a coherence approach because what makes a belief system justified, on this view, is precisely its coherence.

Second, the proposal that a singular belief is justified merely in virtue of being a member of a justified totality can be questioned because, plausibly, a belief can be a member of a sufficiently coherent system without in any way adding to the coherence of that system, e.g., if the belief is the only member which
This fact raises the question of what status those special beliefs have.

sources.annotation: Explains holistic justification, competing coherence measures, and the precise limits of claims connecting coherence with truth.

evidence.excerpt: We often provide reasons for the things we believe in order to justify holding the beliefs.
If both (1) and (2) are true, then the chain of reasons for any belief is potentially infinite, that is, potentially unlimited.
On this alternative reading, these coherentists don’t deny (1), because (1) concerns the structure, not the source, of probative reasons.

For example, the relevant foundationalist property could be that the belief merely reports the contents of sensations or memories; or it could be that the belief is produced by a reliable cognitive faculty.
And once a reason is challenged, then on pain of arbitrariness, a further reason must be produced in order for the challenged reason to serve as a good reason for a belief.
As mentioned above, infinitists reject the form of coherentism – sometimes called “linear coherentism” – that endorses question-begging, circular reasoning.
Holistic coherentism holds that individual beliefs are justified only in virtue of their membership in a coherent set of beliefs.
This is the pattern: There are three possible, non-skeptical solutions to the regress problem: foundationalism, coherentism and infinitism.

sources.annotation: Distinguishes an indefinitely available chain from a completed infinite argument and introduces reason-enhanced justification.
